content: Pantothenic acid, also known as vitamin B5, is a water-soluble vitamin essential for sustaining life. It is required for the synthesis of coenzyme A (CoA), which plays a critical role in the metabolism and synthesis of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. Chemically, pantothenic acid is an amide formed between D-pantoate and beta-alanine. Its name is derived from the Greek word pantothen, meaning from everywhere, as small amounts of pantothenic acid are found in nearly all foods, with higher concentrations in whole grain cereals, legumes, eggs, meat, and royal jelly. It is commonly available in the form of its alcohol analog, pantothenol (a provitamin), or as calcium pantothenate. Only the dextrorotatory (D) isomer of pantothenic acid exhibits biological activity, while the levorotatory (L) form may antagonize the effects of the active isomer. Pantothenic acid is essential for the synthesis of coenzyme A, which functions as an acyl group carrier to form acetyl-CoA and other related compounds. This process facilitates the transport of carbon atoms within cells, which is vital for cellular respiration and the biosynthesis of key compounds such as fatty acids, cholesterol, and acetylcholine. Due to its involvement in numerous critical biological processes, pantothenic acid is considered essential for all forms of life. Deficiencies in this vitamin can lead to a wide range of effects. Pantothenic acid is present in most foods in small quantities, with higher levels found in whole grains and eggs. It is also available in dietary supplements, often as calcium-D-pantothenate, and some companies have begun adding it to beverages. Recent studies suggest that gut bacteria in humans may also produce pantothenic acid. Pantothenate, in the form of pantethine, is considered the more active form of vitamin B5 in the body. However, it is unstable at high temperatures or during prolonged storage, so calcium pantothenate is the more commonly used form in dietary supplements. The recommended daily allowance (RDA) in the United Kingdom is 6 mg/day. Deficiency of pantothenic acid is extremely rare and has not been extensively studied. In the few documented cases, such as in individuals experiencing starvation or in limited volunteer trials, symptoms were reversible upon reintroduction of pantothenic acid. Symptoms of deficiency are similar to those of other B vitamin deficiencies and are generally mild, including fatigue, allergies, nausea, and abdominal pain. In rare cases, more severe but reversible conditions, such as adrenal insufficiency and hepatic encephalopathy, have been observed. A notable symptom reported in deficiency cases is a painful burning sensation in the feet, which was also documented in malnourished prisoners of war. Pantothenic acid has been incorporated into various cosmetic products, including shampoos, due to findings in mouse models that severe deficiency could lead to skin irritation and loss of hair color. However, human trials have shown no significant benefits from these products, yet they continue to be marketed with pantothenic acid additives. In the late 1990s, a small study by Dr. Lit-Hung Leung suggested that high doses of vitamin B5 could treat acne vulgaris and reduce pore size. Dr. Leung proposed a mechanism in which CoA regulates hormones and fatty acids, and insufficient pantothenic acid leads to a preference for androgen production, causing fatty acid buildup and excretion through sebaceous glands, resulting in acne. The study involved 45 Asian males and 55 Asian females who were given 10-20 g of pantothenic acid daily (80% orally and 20% topically). Improvement in acne was noted within one week to one month. However, critics have pointed out flaws in the study, including the lack of a double-blind placebo-controlled trial. To date, this remains the only study examining the effect of vitamin B5 on acne, and most dermatologists do not prescribe high-dose pantothenic acid. Additionally, there is no evidence supporting the proposed regulation of androgens by acetyl-CoA under stress or limited availability, as fatty acids are also essential for life. Pantothenic acid has also been studied in combination with alpha-lipoic acid for diabetic peripheral polyneuropathy. In one study, 28 out of 33 patients (84.8%) previously treated with alpha-lipoic acid reported further improvement when pantothenic acid was added. The theoretical basis for this combination is that both substances act at different sites in pyruvate metabolism, making them more effective together than individually. Clinical findings suggest that diabetic neuropathy may be associated with latent prediabetic metabolic disturbances and that symptoms can be favorably influenced by this combination therapy, even in poorly controlled diabetes. Vitamin B5 supplements are widely marketed for acne treatment, but the recommended treatment regimen can be challenging and expensive. Some protocols suggest starting with 5 g daily for the first three days, then increasing to 10 g daily for three months. Given that the largest available pill is 1 g, this could require taking 10 or more pills daily, with an average cost of $10 for a bottle of 200 tablets. Powdered forms of B5, which can be dissolved in water, are generally cheaper and more convenient for some individuals. After three months, many users reduce the dose to 3-5 g daily, with some claiming that 1 g/day is sufficient. Synonyms for pantothenic acid include pantothenate, vitamin B5, and Vilantae (a brand name for the supplement when used to treat acne).
